THE ML GUIDE
FOR EVERY ENGINEER
What to learn, where to start, and why it matters
— based on YOUR type of engineering
By @1nska
NYU Shanghai — 2026
@1nska  •  The ML Guide for Every Engineer  •  Page 2
Why Every Engineer Needs ML
Machine learning isn't just a CS thing anymore. It's becoming the layer that sits on top of every
engineering discipline. Mechanical engineers use it to predict equipment failures before they happen.
Electrical engineers use it to optimize power grids in real time. Civil engineers use it to model
structural integrity under conditions no equation can fully capture.
The engineers who learn ML now won't just be better engineers — they'll be the ones leading
projects, starting companies, and solving problems that were previously considered unsolvable.
This guide is designed to be practical, not academic. For each engineering
discipline, you'll get: why ML matters for your field, what to learn first, which tools to
use, and a starter project to build.
@1nska  •  The ML Guide for Every Engineer  •  Page 3
The ML Foundation (For Everyone)
Regardless of your discipline, these fundamentals apply to every engineer getting started with ML.
Don't overthink this part — you don't need a PhD in statistics. You need enough to be dangerous.
Core concepts to understand first:
• Supervised vs. unsupervised learning — know when to use each
• Regression vs. classification — the two most common problem types
• Training, validation, and test data — why you split your data and how
• Overfitting — the #1 mistake beginners make
• Feature engineering — often more important than the model itself
The learning path (in order):
• Week 1–2: Python basics (if you don't already know it). Use Python for Everybody (free) or
Codecademy.
• Week 3–5: Andrew Ng's Machine Learning Specialization on Coursera. The gold standard intro.
Do the assignments.
• Week 6–8: Pick ONE project from your discipline section below and build it. Learning by
building beats courses every time.
• Week 9+: Go deeper into the specific ML subfield that applies to your discipline (see your
section).
Pro tip: You don't need to master ML theory. You need to know enough to frame
your engineering problems as ML problems, choose the right approach, and
implement a working solution. That's it.

Your Discipline-Specific Roadmap
Find your engineering type below. Each section gives you a focused path — no fluff, just what you
need.
Mechanical Engineering
Why ML matters here:
Predictive maintenance alone is a massive industry. ML models can predict when a machine will fail
based on sensor data — vibration, temperature, pressure — saving millions in downtime. Beyond
that, generative design uses ML to explore thousands of design variations to find optimal shapes and
structures that no human would think of.
Start with:
• Time-series analysis — your sensor data is sequential, so learn how to work with it
• Regression models — predicting continuous values (temperature, stress, wear)
• Anomaly detection — flagging when something is about to break
Key tools:
• scikit-learn — your first stop for classical ML models
• TensorFlow / PyTorch — for deeper neural network models
• MATLAB ML Toolbox — if you're already in the MATLAB ecosystem
• PySpark — for working with large-scale sensor datasets
Starter project: Build a predictive maintenance model using a public bearing
vibration dataset (NASA's bearing dataset is free). Train a model to predict remaining
useful life of a component.
Electrical Engineering
Why ML matters here:
Signal processing and ML are a natural fit. From optimizing power grid loads to designing smarter
circuits, ML is already deeply embedded in EE. If you work with signals, images, or any kind of
waveform data, neural networks can find patterns your traditional filters miss.
Start with:
• Signal classification — identifying patterns in waveforms
@1nska  •  The ML Guide for Every Engineer  •  Page 5
• Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) — not just for images; great for spectrograms and
signal data
• Reinforcement learning basics — for control systems and optimization
Key tools:
• PyTorch — the go-to for signal and research-oriented ML
• scipy.signal — preprocessing your signals before feeding to ML
• Edge Impulse — deploy ML models on embedded hardware
• TinyML — ML that runs on microcontrollers
Starter project: Build a signal classifier that can distinguish between different types
of electrical faults using publicly available power quality datasets. Deploy it on an
Arduino or Raspberry Pi for bonus points.
Civil / Structural Engineering
Why ML matters here:
Infrastructure generates massive amounts of data — strain gauges, traffic sensors, weather patterns,
soil tests. ML can process all of it simultaneously to predict structural health, optimize traffic flow, and
estimate construction costs more accurately than traditional methods.
Start with:
• Regression models — for cost estimation and load prediction
• Computer vision — crack detection, site monitoring, progress tracking
• Geospatial data analysis — combining satellite imagery with ground data
Key tools:
• scikit-learn — for tabular data (soil data, cost estimates, measurements)
• OpenCV + YOLO — for visual inspection and crack detection
• Google Earth Engine — for satellite imagery analysis
• Pandas + GeoPandas — for geospatial data wrangling
Starter project: Train a computer vision model to detect cracks in concrete surfaces
using the public SDNET2018 dataset. This is directly applicable to bridge and
building inspection.

Chemical / Process Engineering
Why ML matters here:
Chemical processes are complex, nonlinear systems with dozens of interacting variables. ML excels
at modeling these relationships — predicting reaction yields, optimizing process parameters, and
catching quality issues before they become expensive. Pharma and materials science are being
transformed by ML-driven discovery.
Start with:
• Process optimization — finding optimal operating conditions from historical data
• Soft sensors — predicting hard-to-measure variables from easy-to-measure ones
• Molecular property prediction — emerging and high-impact area
Key tools:
• scikit-learn — classical models for process data
• RDKit — molecular informatics and cheminformatics
• DeepChem — deep learning specifically for chemistry applications
• Aspen + Python API — connecting ML to process simulation
Starter project: Use a public dataset of chemical reactions (try the USPTO reaction
dataset) to build a model that predicts reaction yield based on input conditions. Start
with a simple random forest, then try a neural network.
Biomedical Engineering
Why ML matters here:
Medical imaging, wearable sensors, genomics — biomedical engineering is one of the fields most
transformed by ML. From detecting tumors in X-rays to predicting patient outcomes from wearable
data, the applications are immediate and the demand for engineers who can bridge biology and ML is
enormous.
Start with:
• Medical image classification — detecting anomalies in scans
• Time-series from wearables — heart rate, EEG, EMG signal analysis
• Natural Language Processing — extracting insights from clinical notes
Key tools:
• PyTorch + MONAI — purpose-built for medical imaging AI
@1nska  •  The ML Guide for Every Engineer  •  Page 7
• TensorFlow Lite — deploying models on wearable devices
• BioPython — for genomics and bioinformatics
• Hugging Face — for NLP models on clinical text
Starter project: Build an ECG classification model using the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia
Database (free on PhysioNet). Train a model to distinguish normal heartbeats from
arrhythmias.
Software / Computer Engineering
Why ML matters here:
You might think you already know this — but there's a difference between using ML APIs and
understanding how to design ML systems. As a software engineer, your advantage is that you
already know how to code and ship products. The gap is in ML system design, model selection, and
data pipeline architecture.
Start with:
• ML system design — how to architect production ML pipelines
• MLOps — model versioning, monitoring, retraining in production
• Deep learning — transformers, LLMs, and their practical applications
Key tools:
• PyTorch — the standard for research and increasingly for production
• MLflow / Weights & Biases — experiment tracking and model management
• Hugging Face — transformers and pre-trained models
• LangChain / LlamaIndex — building applications on top of LLMs
Starter project: Build a full ML-powered feature for a product: data pipeline, model
training, API endpoint, and monitoring. Use a real dataset, deploy it, and track
performance. The full stack experience is what sets you apart.

Free Resources to Get Started
You don't need to spend money to learn ML. Here are the best free resources, organized by stage.
Courses
• Andrew Ng's ML Specialization (Coursera) — the best starting point, period
• fast.ai Practical Deep Learning — top-down approach, build things from day one
• MIT OpenCourseWare 6.036 — more rigorous, great if you want deeper math foundations
• Google's ML Crash Course — quick, practical, excellent for engineers
• Stanford CS229 (YouTube) — the classic graduate-level course, free on YouTube
Practice platforms
• Kaggle — competitions, datasets, and notebooks. Start with their "Learn" courses
• Google Colab — free GPU notebooks. No setup required
• Papers With Code — find state-of-the-art models with implementations
• Hugging Face — pre-trained models you can fine-tune for your domain
Books (free online)
• Hands-On ML with Scikit-Learn, Keras & TensorFlow by Aurélien Géron — practical and
project-driven
• Deep Learning by Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville — the deep learning bible (free at
deeplearningbook.org)
• Pattern Recognition and ML by Bishop — for those who want the math

The 8-Week Kickstart Plan
Here's a week-by-week plan to go from zero ML knowledge to having a working project on your
resume. Spend 5–8 hours per week. Consistency beats intensity.

Week 1
Setup & Python review
Install Python, set up Jupyter/Colab, review NumPy and Pandas basics. If you
already know Python, skip to data manipulation exercises.

Week 2
ML fundamentals
Start Andrew Ng's course or fast.ai. Focus on understanding supervised
learning, linear regression, and classification. Don't get stuck on math —
understand the intuition.

Week 3
Your first model
Pick a simple dataset from Kaggle (house prices, titanic). Build a model from
scratch using scikit-learn. Submit to a Kaggle competition.

Week 4
Deeper models
Learn decision trees, random forests, and gradient boosting. These are the
workhorses of real-world ML. Practice feature engineering.

Week 5
Intro to deep learning
Learn what neural networks are and when to use them. Build a simple image
classifier or text classifier using PyTorch or TensorFlow.

Week 6
Domain-specific deep dive
Go to YOUR discipline section in this guide. Start the recommended project.
Research how ML is being used in your specific field.

Week 7
Build your project
Dedicate this week to building and iterating on your domain project. Document
everything — this becomes your portfolio piece.

Week 8
Polish & share
Clean up your project code, write a README, publish on GitHub. Post about
what you built on LinkedIn or Instagram. You now have proof you can do this.

Now Go Build Something
The best way to learn ML is to apply it to a problem you actually care about. Don't wait until you feel
"ready" — you won't. Pick the starter project for your discipline, open a Colab notebook, and start.
You'll learn more in one weekend of building than in a month of watching tutorials.
If you want more guides like this — on building startups, switching career paths, or bridging business
and engineering — follow me on Instagram. I'm documenting the entire journey.
Follow @1nska on Instagram for more guides, build logs, and real talk about
building as a student. DM me "PROJECT" and I'll help you pick the right ML starter
project for your field.
